strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-motivated gap: GRPO-style critic-free RL aggregates rollout contributions across heterogeneous tasks without regulating disparities in advantage magnitudes, which the authors illustrate empirically (Fig. 7 advantage distributions differing across tasks; Fig. 6 contribution signals varying by orders of magnitude).

The core mechanism is cleanly designed and clearly presented: reciprocal ratio-to-geometric-mean modulation factors with a proven geometric-mean-of-1 property (App. D.2), which gives a principled argument that modulation does not systematically inflate or shrink the global update scale — a nice property absent from naive 1/p reweighting, which the ablation confirms (sustained ~2.5x net amplification without geometric centering).

The RL algorithm comparison is fair and reasonably controlled: GRPO, RLOO, GPG, and RE++ are all trained on the same benchmark, base model (Qwen2.5-Omni-7B), rollout counts, batch sizes, and reward design, using a standard package (VERL).

Component-wise ablations (structured modulation, sample-level modulation, inertial control) are supported by mechanistic analyses (advantage distribution narrowing, modulation factor trajectories, relative task advantage vs. rewards on a weak task), rather than only end-task numbers.

Evaluation goes beyond multitask performance: zero-shot transfer to held-out datasets (AV-ASD, IEMOCAP) and qualitative reasoning-trace analyses provide converging evidence, and the paper is forthcoming about trade-offs (e.g., lower recall but higher precision on AUT).
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is modest. HARPO is essentially advantage/loss reweighting at two granularities with EMA smoothing — closely related to classical multitask loss balancing (Kendall et al., Yu et al.), difficulty-aware reweighting (GRPO-LEAD), and DAPO-style normalization tricks. The paper positions these as related but does not offer theoretical analysis of when the modulation converges to a desirable fixed point or how it interacts with PPO clipping and the ratio-based importance weights (modulated advantages change the effective clipping region in ways not analyzed).

Generality of the method is untested beyond a single benchmark. All experiments use the Human Behavior Atlas; there is no experiment on standard RL reasoning or general multitask settings. It is unclear whether the gains stem from the method itself or from properties of this particular benchmark/reward distribution.

No variance or significance reporting. RL runs are notoriously high variance, yet the paper appears to report single runs. Many margins in Table 1 are small (HARPO avg. rank 1.70 vs. 2.50 for RLOO/GPG; several per-task differences within ~1 point), so claims of 'most consistently strong performance' are not statistically supported.

Internal inconsistencies in reported numbers undermine confidence: the average rank for HARPO is 1.70 in Table 1 but 1.90 in Tables 3 and 5; Figure 1 captions list GRPO HUM F1 as 27.60 in one place and 27.56 in another; Table 6 (per-dataset ablation breakdown) is badly garbled and unreadable.

Some design choices appear post-hoc and weakly justified, e.g., dropping KL regularization for all algorithms is described as motivated by HARPO's regularization effect, but this conflates the method's contribution with a confounding training configuration change.

The headline model comparisons (models section of Table 1) are partly taken from a prior paper's runs rather than re-evaluated under identical conditions (only Qwen3-VL was run by the authors), weakening the model-level claims; the QA/social tasks rely on LLM-judge and cosine-similarity rewards/metrics, which are noisy.

The causal story in Fig. 4 (advantage amplification causing reward improvement on SAR) is correlational and restricted to one task; sample-level modulation is explicitly reported to not help EMO, INT, and SOC, tempering the generality of the mechanism's benefit.
Reproducibility is limited at review time: models, code, and reasoning traces are promised only 'after the review process', so central claims cannot currently be independently verified.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and underexplored problem: critic-free reasoning RL methods (GRPO and variants) do not explicitly handle heterogeneous learning signals across tasks, and multitask balancing techniques have not been adapted to this setting.

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this area: 10 behavioral tasks spanning 13 datasets, a comparison against four recent critic-free RL baselines (RLOO, RE++, GPG, GRPO) under an identical reward design and base model, zero-shot transfer to two held-out datasets (AUT, SER), qualitative reasoning-trace analysis, and component-wise ablations (structured modulation, sample-level modulation, inertial control) with supporting training-dynamics plots (Figs. 4-6).

The empirical analysis in Sec. 4.5 is a genuine strength: the SAR case study (Fig. 4) directly links the relative task advantage statistic to reward trajectories, and the ablations are accompanied by mechanistic plots (advantage distribution narrowing, modulation factor stability) rather than only end metrics.

The geometric-centering construction is cleanly derived (App. D.2), and the failure mode of the naive 1/p(t) variant (sustained net amplification of advantages, geometric mean above 2.5 in Fig. 6) is well documented and instructive.
The method is described at sufficient implementation detail (Algorithm 1, hyperparameters in App. C, VERL-based implementation) that reimplementation is plausible.
weaknesses: Weak statistical evidence for the central claim. All RL comparisons appear to be single runs with no seeds, no confidence intervals, and no significance testing. The headline result — HARPO's average rank of 1.70 vs. 2.50 for RLOO and GPG — rests on small per-task margins on a benchmark where RL training is known to be high-variance (the authors themselves cite Henderson et al., 2018 on this instability). Notably, HARPO is *worse* than RLOO on SOC (25.40 vs 29.54) and NVC (14.54 vs 16.28), so 'most consistently strong' is an interpretation of rank aggregation rather than a robust empirical finding.

The ablation evidence for the core 'structured modulation' component is very thin: removing geometric centering changes the average rank only from 1.90 to 2.00, which is within plausible run-to-run noise for an unreplicated experiment. The paper's own analysis also concedes that sample-level modulation shows 'no explicit improvements' for EMO, INT, and SOC. The ablations therefore do not convincingly establish that the full mechanism is necessary.

Baseline treatment raises fairness concerns. HARPO omits the KL regularization term ('motivated by HARPO's advantage modulation') while baselines keep their original configurations, and baseline hyperparameters are reused from their original papers rather than tuned on this multimodal behavioral benchmark. The claimed improvements may partly reflect these asymmetries rather than the advantage modulation itself; a GRPO run without KL and with matched tuning would be the appropriate control.

Thin theoretical grounding. The geometric-mean argument (App. D.2) guarantees only that the product of modulation factors equals 1; it does not establish that the effective update size or trust-region geometry is preserved, since advantage rescaling changes gradient directions non-uniformly and interacts with PPO clipping in ways the paper does not analyze. The claimed mitigation of 'unintended influence on the global step size' is asserted rather than shown.

The method is close to existing difficulty-aware advantage reweighting (e.g., GRPO-LEAD, which the authors cite as shaping 'difficulty-aware reweighting') and to classical multitask balancing (Kendall et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2020). The paper does not compare against or clearly delineate HARPO from these approaches, and related work engagement remains superficial.

Headline numbers are selectively favorable. The 'up to +42.29% over GRPO' is driven by a single task (HUM) where GRPO collapses (27.56 vs 69.85), and the '+16.85%' multitask gain is relative, not absolute. Absolute task-level improvements over the strongest baseline (RLOO/GPG) are modest on most tasks.

Limited external validity. The method is motivated as general ('learning across heterogeneous tasks') but is evaluated on exactly one benchmark. There is no evidence that HARPO transfers to standard heterogeneous RL settings (e.g., math/code reasoning mixtures), leaving open whether the gains are benchmark-specific.

Ethics treatment is inadequate for the application domain. The model performs depression, anxiety, PTSD, and autism-related behavioral detection — sensitive mental-health inference — yet the Impact Statement is boilerplate ('none which we feel must be specifically highlighted here'). Potential harms (misdiagnosis, stigma, privacy of clinical data such as DAIC-WOZ) are not discussed.

Reproducibility is currently limited: models, code, and reasoning traces are promised only 'after the review process,' so the central results cannot be verified at submission time. Evaluation of the QA tasks also depends on an LLM judge (GPT-5-nano), introducing an additional unquantified source of evaluation noise.

The comparison with prior behavioral models (Tab. 1) mixes numbers taken from the Human Behavior Atlas paper with newly run evaluations, and the improvement over OmniSapiens-7B RL conflates the RL algorithm change with any other training-recipe differences, making attribution of the model-level gains to HARPO alone uncertain.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: balancing learning signals across heterogeneous behavioral tasks in critic-free reasoning RL, a genuine gap between recent GRPO-style methods and multitask learning literature

HARPO's modulation mechanism is principled and cleanly presented: contribution signals from advantage magnitudes, geometric-mean referencing with an appendix derivation showing modulation factors have geometric mean exactly 1 (preventing unintended global step-size scaling), and inertial smoothing

Fair algorithmic comparison: all RL baselines (GRPO, RLOO, RE++, GPG) are retrained on the same benchmark, base model (Qwen2.5-Omni-7B), and identical reward design, rather than comparing against numbers copied from other papers

Thoughtful ablations with mechanistic analysis: the relative-task-advantage tracking (Fig. 4), modulation factor trajectories with/without inertial control (Fig. 5), and geometric-mean analysis of the 1/p(t) variant (Fig. 6) go beyond simple before/after numbers and connect design choices to training dynamics

Evaluation spans multitask performance, zero-shot transfer to two held-out datasets (AUT, SER), and qualitative reasoning-trace analysis, giving multiple angles on the claim that balanced optimization improves generalization
weaknesses: HARPO is positioned as a general RL method for heterogeneous tasks, but it is validated on a single benchmark (Human Behavior Atlas) with a single base model; no evidence it helps on standard reasoning benchmarks or other multitask RL settings, so the generality of the method is untested

Results appear to come from single runs with no seeds, variance, or statistical significance reported; RL training is notoriously high-variance, and the key ablation deltas are small (HARPO avg. rank 1.90 vs. w/o structured modulation 2.00), making it hard to judge whether the structured-modulation component genuinely matters

The narrative slightly overstates ablation results: the 'w/o structured modulation' variant actually outperforms full HARPO on several tasks (SAR, SOC, NVC) and several datasets, and full HARPO's SOC score (25.40) is below RLOO (29.54) and GPG (27.93), suggesting modulation may suppress learning on some tasks; this is acknowledged only briefly

Several tables appear garbled or internally inconsistent: Table 7's dataset-level values seem misaligned with the task-level averages in Table 1 (e.g., EMO for OmniSapiens-2.0 is 76.55 in Table 1 but the constituent values in Table 7 include 85.80), Table 6 likewise appears misaligned, and Fig. 1 quotes GRPO HUM F1 as 27.60 vs. 27.56 elsewhere; the headline +16.85% claim is not clearly traceable to a specific comparison
Three of ten tasks (SOC, INT, NVC) rely on an LLM judge (GPT-5 nano), introducing evaluation noise and potential bias that is not addressed (e.g., no judge-agreement analysis)

The paper lacks an explicit limitations section; failure modes of advantage modulation (e.g., amplifying noisy weak tasks, or harm to tasks that genuinely require large advantage signals) are not discussed, and the Impact Statement is boilerplate despite the model addressing mental-health detection (depression, anxiety, PTSD), which deserves more careful ethical treatment

Reproducibility is limited: code and models are promised only 'after the review process'; the many hyperparameters introduced by HARPO (beta_rho, beta_s, batch sampling structure) are only partially specified (0.95 for both), with no sensitivity analysis

GRPO-LEAD, the closest related difficulty-aware reweighting method, is cited but not included in the empirical comparison, which weakens the claim that HARPO is the strongest heterogeneity-aware approach

strengths: Well-motivated problem: the paper identifies a real and concrete issue — heterogeneous behavioral tasks induce systematically different advantage magnitudes under GRPO, which are then shown empirically (App. F.3) to skew policy updates.

HARPO is simple, clearly specified, and easy to reproduce: the contribution signals (Eq. 6-7), geometric-mean references (Eq. 8-9), and inertial smoothing (Eq. 11) are fully formalized, with Algorithm 1 and a derivation (App. E.2) showing the modulation factors have unit geometric mean, preventing global step-size drift.

Algorithm comparison is reasonably fair: all RL baselines (GRPO, RLOO, RE++, GPG, EMAGRPO) are trained on the same Human Behavior Atlas benchmark, with the same base model (Qwen2.5-Omni-7B), identical reward design, and hyperparameters from original papers, mitigating the common risk of strawman RL comparisons.

Thorough component ablations (Tab. 5, 7, 8) with mechanistic analysis: the geometric-centering, sample-level, and inertial-control components are each isolated, and the analysis (Figs. 2, 3, 6, 7) connects modulation behavior to task performance rather than only reporting end scores.

Evaluation spans three dimensions (multitask, zero-shot generalization on held-out datasets, reasoning interpretability), with the interpretability analysis combining automated consistency/paraphrase metrics and a masked human evaluation with detailed instructions provided.

Honest acknowledgment of heterogeneous ablation effects, e.g., that sample-level modulation shows no improvement for EMO, INT, SOC, and that the generalization mechanism is conjectural, left to future work.
weaknesses: No statistical uncertainty anywhere: all results appear to be single runs (single seed per algorithm and ablation). Given the acknowledged high variance of on-policy RL, gains such as avg. rank 1.90 vs 2.00 for the 'w/o structured modulation' ablation, or 2.10 vs 2.90 for GRPO, are within plausible run-to-run noise and cannot be reliably interpreted without multiple seeds or confidence intervals.

The contribution signal is a crude heuristic: p is the mean absolute group-normalized advantage, which ignores the sign/direction of advantages and the actual gradient norm. Downsampling high-|advantage| samples while upscaling low-|advantage| ones plausibly amplifies noisy, uninformative rollouts and slows learning from the most informative ones; the paper offers no theoretical or controlled empirical justification that |advantage| magnitude is a valid proxy for 'disproportionate influence' rather than informative learning signal.

Novelty is incremental: difficulty-aware and importance-based reweighting of GRPO advantages exists (GRPO-LEAD, EMAGRPO, which is compared), and the geometric-centering + EMA construction is a combination of standard techniques (reciprocal normalization, multiplicative-weights smoothing). The framing as a foundation-model contribution inflates a fairly modest algorithmic delta.

Several baseline results look pathological but are not investigated: RE++ collapsing to 5.01 on INT and GRPO to 27.56 on HUM (vs ~50-70 for others) suggest training instability or tuning mismatches, and HARPO's headline +42.29% over GRPO is driven by these collapse cases. Additionally, PTSD is identical (98.39) across nearly all methods, suggesting metric saturation/label imbalance that limits what Tab. 1 can distinguish.

The mechanism claim in Fig. 2 (modulation sustains learning for weak tasks) is a correlational, post-hoc observation from a single run on one task (SAR); no causal intervention (e.g., modulation schedule ablation on the same task) supports the causal interpretation.

Human evaluation is small-scale: 3 annotators, no reported number of comparison instances, no inter-annotator agreement, and no statistical testing; conclusions about interpretability gains rest heavily on this thin evidence plus one case study (Fig. 1). The interpretability argument would also benefit from noting that concise (19.86 token) traces may trade off completeness, which the paper asserts rather than tests.

Clinical/ethical treatment is superficial: the model targets depression, anxiety, PTSD, and autism detection, yet the impact statement is boilerplate and there is no limitations section discussing risks of deployment in behavioral health, dataset biases, or validity of LLM-judge grading (GPT-5 nano) for socially sensitive tasks.

Generalization claims rest on five held-out datasets where several baselines perform poorly (e.g., HumanOmniV2 at 21.97 on IDR); relative improvements against a stronger, uniformly competitive baseline are not established, and model-level results in Tab. 1 are largely inherited from the prior benchmark paper rather than re-run.

Presentation issues reduce polish: broken link in the abstract ('Our model and codes can be found at'), typos ('exhbit', 'atleast', 'simulateneously'), formatting inconsistencies in Tab. 8/9 headers, and reasoning traces promised only 'after the review process' weaken reproducibility at submission time.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical scope: evaluation spans 10 behavioral tasks over 13 datasets (Tab. 1, 6, 9) plus 5 held-out zero-shot tasks, and the RL algorithm comparison is commendably controlled — same backbone (Qwen2.5-Omni-7B), same Human Behavior Atlas data, and identical reward design across GRPO, RLOO, RE++, GPG, and EMAGRPO (App. C.1).

The core idea is sensible and clearly motivated: advantage magnitudes in GRPO scale each rollout's gradient contribution (Eqs. 4–5), so rebalancing them across heterogeneous tasks is a plausible lever for multitask RL; the geometric-mean construction (Eqs. 8–10) with a proof that modulation factors have geometric mean 1 (App. E.2) is a clean design that prevents global step-size drift.

Honest mechanistic analysis beyond headline numbers: ablations of each component (Tab. 5, 7, 8), training-dynamics plots connecting relative task advantage to reward trajectories for a weak task (Fig. 2), advantage distribution analysis (Fig. 3, 7), and modulation factor trajectories (Fig. 6) give the reader a genuine picture of why the method behaves as claimed.

Multi-dimensional interpretability evaluation (Tab. 3, 4) with a described protocol: consistency, paraphrase robustness, trace length, and a masked pairwise human study with annotators outside the authorship (App. D).
Component-wise insight is candid in places: the paper acknowledges sample-level modulation does not help all tasks (EMO, INT, SOC) and that inertial control effects are task-dependent (Sec. 4.4).
weaknesses: Evidence for the central claim is statistically weak. All results appear to come from single training runs with no seeds, variance, or significance reporting, despite the authors themselves noting the 'high variance and non-stationarity of on-policy sampling' (App. C.1). The headline algorithm comparison rests on average ranks of 1.90 (HARPO) vs. 2.10 (EMAGRPO) vs. 2.80 (RLOO) — a gap of 0.2 rank positions is well within plausible run-to-run noise, and the structured-modulation ablation (1.90 vs. 2.00) is even thinner.

Suspicious and degenerate results undermine confidence in the evaluation: PTSD scores are 98.39 for five of six RL methods and for the SFT/BAM variants (100.00), suggesting a saturated or degenerate majority-class prediction on a 189-sample dataset (DAIC-WOZ) rather than meaningful learning; DEP on DAIC-WOZ has only 189 samples yet drives a full task column. These pathologies are not discussed.

The contribution proxy is theoretically under-motivated and has a numerical hazard. Average absolute advantage conflates gradient contribution magnitude with learning value — samples with high reward variance (arguably the most informative) are systematically downweighted, and the paper offers no analysis of when this helps versus suppresses signal. Worse, p(t)(m,q)=0 when a rollout group has uniform rewards, making s = p̄ref/p unbounded; no clipping or floor is specified, and this instability is never addressed.

Internal inconsistencies weaken the reasoning claims: Tab. 3 celebrates HARPO's extreme conciseness (19.86 tokens vs. 57.69 next best) as an interpretability win, while Sec. 4.4/Fig. 4 argue that HARPO's longer, more varied reasoning is what improves HUM/SAR. Fig. 5 directly contradicts the paper's own narrative — HARPO's 'reasoning' for the sarcasm example is literally the single word 'Sarcasm', yet it is presented as evidence of richer, contextually grounded reasoning. Ultra-short traces plus the highest accuracy are also consistent with shortcut behavior, not interpretability.

The human evaluation is small and weakly controlled: three annotators, no reported inter-annotator agreement, no sample count per comparison, and criteria ('work quickly and rely on your first judgment') that invite bias. Win rates excluding ties of 68.5–99.2% are reported without any uncertainty quantification.

Zero-shot generalization (Tab. 2) compares against only four baselines, omits the other RL algorithms evaluated in Tab. 1, and the gains (e.g., 39.91 vs. 38.05 AUT) are modest; the causal story that 'uniform learning promotes transferable features' is explicitly deferred to future work, so the generalization claim is correlational at best.

Ethics treatment is inadequate for the application domain. The model performs depression, anxiety, PTSD, and autism detection and the paper invokes 'critical behavioral applications (i.e., health)' as motivation, yet the Impact Statement is boilerplate and there is no discussion of clinical misdiagnosis risk, dataset consent (e.g., DAIC-WOZ clinical interviews), or suitability of a 7B general model for such inferences.

Reproducibility is partially promised rather than delivered: the repository link in the abstract is empty, reasoning traces are only 'publicly available after the review process', and key details (e.g., baseline configurations reused from original papers, the LLM-judge prompts for SOC/INT/NVC) are outsourced to external sources. GPT-5-nano judging also makes a central metric non-deterministic and version-dependent.

Originality is moderate: advantage reweighting by difficulty/magnitude is well-trodden (GRPO-LEAD, DAPO-style penalties, EMAGRPO for multitask balancing), and HARPO is best viewed as a combination of known rebalancing ideas (reciprocal scaling + EMA smoothing) applied to a new domain. The application is useful, but the methodological novelty is incremental.

Presentational issues: claims like 'gains of up to +42.29%' are drawn from single-task comparisons against the worst baseline on that task (HUM: 69.85 vs. 27.56), which inflates the headline; 'Gemma 4-E4B' appears alongside a Gemma-3 citation; and the abstract's release statement is incomplete.

strengths: The core problem is well-motivated and clearly diagnosed: the paper provides empirical evidence (Fig. 6/7, App. F.3) that advantage distributions differ systematically across behavioral tasks under GRPO, which directly motivates HARPO's advantage modulation.

The RL algorithm comparison is unusually fair: all baselines (GRPO, RLOO, RE++, GPG, EMAGRPO) are trained on the same Human Behavior Atlas benchmark, same base model (Qwen2.5-Omni-7B), identical reward design, and a common implementation (VERL), reducing confounds from implementation differences.

Comprehensive ablations isolate each component of HARPO (structured geometric modulation, sample-level modulation, inertial control), and the mechanistic analyses (Fig. 2 on SAR relative task advantage, Fig. 3 on advantage distributions and modulation factor dynamics) connect design choices to training behavior rather than only reporting final numbers.

Evaluation goes beyond accuracy: zero-shot generalization on five held-out tasks, automated consistency/paraphrase/token-efficiency metrics, and a masked three-annotator pairwise human evaluation with instructions included, plus a promised release of model, code, and reasoning traces.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported: hyperparameters, reward formulas, decoding configurations, and dataset/metric tables (Tab. 6, App. C) are specified in detail.
weaknesses: No variance reporting: results appear to come from single runs, yet RL fine-tuning is notoriously high-variance. Key claims rest on small rank differences (e.g., HARPO avg. rank 1.90 vs. 2.00 for the 'w/o structured modulation' ablation, and 2.10 vs. 2.80 for RLOO) with no seeds, standard deviations, or significance testing.

The central theoretical claim—that mean absolute advantage is a valid proxy for 'contribution to the policy update' and that equalizing it is desirable—is asserted rather than analyzed. Reciprocally upscaling low-contribution (potentially noisy) samples can increase gradient variance; the paper notes narrower advantage distributions but offers no analysis of when balancing helps versus harms (indeed EMO, INT, SOC show no gains from sample-level modulation).

The method is an incremental combination of known ideas: contribution-based/inverse-difficulty advantage reweighting (cf. GRPO-LEAD difficulty-aware reweighting), moving-average task balancing (cf. EMAGRPO), and classical multitask balancing (GradNorm-style), with geometric centering and multiplicative smoothing as the main novel twists. Generalization beyond this single domain/benchmark is not demonstrated.

Interpretability claims are only partially supported: the human evaluation involves only 3 annotators, and near-ceiling win rates (99-100% Tie+Win for concision against every baseline) are suspicious and could reflect format artifacts (shorter traces) rather than genuine explanatory quality; consistency metrics also compare models under different decoding configurations.

Some headline numbers are cherry-picked: 'outperforming GRPO by up to +42.29%' reflects a single task (HUM, 69.85 vs. 27.56) where GRPO evidently collapsed, and average-rank metrics obscure the magnitude and sign of per-task differences (e.g., HARPO loses to EMAGRPO on SAR and to GPG/RLOO on SOC/INT/NVC).

The reward r = (1-w)r_task + w r_fmt + 0.75*r_len is not normalized to a fixed range, meaning reward scale varies with response length across tasks—ironic given the paper's stated concern with heterogeneous reward scales—and this interaction is not analyzed.

Potential confound in the reasoning analyses: HARPO's concise traces (19.86 tokens) may partly reflect optimization pressure from the length penalty interacting with the modulation scheme, but the paper attributes conciseness/consistency to better interpretability without disentangling these.

Ethical treatment is thin: the model performs clinical inferences (depression, anxiety, PTSD, autism detection) with nontrivial error rates, yet the Impact Statement is boilerplate and the paper does not discuss risks of deploying such a model in behavioral-health contexts; the abstract's appeal to 'reliable real-world behavioral applications' exceeds what the evidence establishes.

Minor presentation issues: typos ('intertially', 'exhbit', 'possess a geometric mean'), and Table 1's model-vs-algorithm grouping requires careful reading to avoid unfair comparisons (e.g., OmniSapiens-7B RL numbers differ from the GRPO row despite identical benchmark/reward framing).
